section_summary: This section assembles U.S. diplomatic, military, and FBI reporting on Japanese aircraft procurement, design, production capacity, raw-material supplies, and air strength from 1940 through 1944. Major subjects include attempted purchases of American aircraft through the Caribbean, German aircraft transfers, Zero-fighter characteristics, and competing estimates of Japan’s monthly aircraft output. A substantial 1942 report concludes that captured Southeast Asian tin would have little direct effect on aircraft production, while later British and American assessments debate whether Japanese output was closer to 4,000–5,000 or 12,000–16,000 aircraft annually.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on shipments of equipment to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a letter concerning equipment shipments to Japan in response to a presidential request for information.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a January 2, 1940 letter from Eclipse Aviation, Bendix, N.J., on shipments of equipment to Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum concerning George Burris, airplane salesman
subfiles.from: F. M. Churchill, Acting Assistant Chief of Staff
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports an alleged proposal to route American aircraft and engines to Japan through the Dominican Republic.
subfiles.summary: George Burris, claiming to represent Curtiss-Wright, reportedly said aircraft could reach Japan via the Dominican Republic; the Japanese Navy wanted Wright and Pratt & Whitney engines, Curtiss P-40s and fabric tanks; he lives with NYK agent Himenesu.

subfiles.title: Distribution of the Japanese Army Air Force as of December 1939
subfiles.doc_type: military attaché report with statistical table
subfiles.about: The report transmits a foreign-source tabulation of Japanese Army Air Force units and aircraft.
subfiles.summary: William Meyer forwards a tabulation described as showing the Japanese Army Air Force’s distribution in December 1939. The damaged table lists regiments, squadrons, and aircraft types and gives totals of 34 squadrons and 381 planes.

subfiles.title: Report on George Burris
subfiles.from: Henry A. Barber Jr., Military Attaché
subfiles.about: The report identifies Burris as a Curtiss-Wright mechanic formerly sent to Santo Domingo and discusses efforts to locate him.
subfiles.summary: Military attache: Burris was a Curtiss-Wright mechanic sent to Santo Domingo two years earlier; no trace in Havana, likely in Santo Domingo; surveillance continues.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese air losses in China
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report tabulating Japanese aircraft losses during air combat operations in China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a May 1940 Military Attache report on Japanese air-combat losses in China.

subfiles.title: Characteristics of the Japanese Type Zero fighter and Type 99 bomber
subfiles.about: The memorandum records intelligence on the performance, armament, endurance, and tactics of two Japanese aircraft types.
subfiles.summary: Per a captured pilot, the Zero fighter reaches 300 knots with two 20-mm cannon and two machine guns; the two-seat Type 99 bomber carries three machine guns and 370 kilograms of bombs; both suit carriers, and Japanese air activity in China fell.

subfiles.title: FBI letter and memorandum on Japan’s aeronautical industry
subfiles.about: Hoover transmits information on Japanese industrial production, including the growing employment of women in aircraft factories.
subfiles.summary: FBI memorandum on Japanese aircraft, ship and aluminum production: women increasingly weld and make parts on eleven-hour shifts at 60-75 percent of men's pay, with male trainees scarce because Manchuria and North China pay better.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese procurement of German warplanes
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram about discussions during Matsuoka’s Berlin visit concerning German aircraft for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: talks on supplying Japan German warplanes as compensation for raw materials from the Netherlands East Indies shipped to Germany.

subfiles.title: Aviation statistics: estimated fuel requirements for October 1940
subfiles.from: Assistant General Manager, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company, Japan Division
subfiles.about: The letter transmits two copies of a monthly statement estimating aviation-fuel requirements.
subfiles.summary: Standard-Vacuum's Japan Division sends New York two copies of Statement 12, estimated aviation-fuel needs for October 1940; the statement isn't reproduced.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting aircraft shipments through Dairen
subfiles.about: The telegram reports that approximately 300 unidentified aircraft had entered through Dairen and moved north by rail.
subfiles.summary: Telegram: a consular colleague learned about 300 aircraft of unknown type came through Dairen in a fortnight and went north by rail; sent to Tokyo, Peiping, Mukden and Harbin.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on alleged German aircraft transfers to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram reporting a Soviet military belief that Germany had supplied Japan with approximately 1,500 aircraft.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a British telegram: Soviet military authorities reportedly believed Germany transferred about 1,500 aircraft to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese aircraft-production estimates
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram estimating Japanese aircraft production.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a February 10, 1942 telegram from Switzerland on Japanese aircraft output; the estimate isn't given.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the report on tin and Japanese aircraft production
subfiles.about: Grummon thanks Baxter for supplying the Economics Division report on tin acquisitions and Japanese aircraft production.
subfiles.summary: Stuart Grummon acknowledges Economics Division Report 3, "The Relation of Tin Acquisitions to Airplane Production in Japan," and thanks Baxter.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Economics Division Report No. 3
subfiles.about: Baxter transmits a confidential research report prepared at the request of Air Corps Intelligence.
subfiles.summary: James Baxter sends Grummon the confidential report on tin and Japanese aircraft production, prepared for Air Corps Intelligence.

subfiles.title: The Relation of Tin Acquisitions to Airplane Production in Japan
subfiles.from: Economics Division, Research and Analysis Branch, Office of the Coordinator of Information
subfiles.about: The report assesses whether Japan’s seizure of major Southeast Asian tin-producing areas could materially increase aircraft production.
subfiles.summary: The report estimates that Japanese-controlled territories had prewar capacity for about 175,000 long tons of tin annually, although damaged mines and smelters would take months to restore. It concludes that Japan had little use for such a large tin supply because aircraft employed tin only in limited solders, alloys, and engine parts. Aluminum and bauxite supplies were judged ample for production of 400 aircraft per month, while machine-tool capacity and skilled labor were considered more important constraints on expansion.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file 894.248
subfiles.about: The form records the temporary charging or removal of material from file 894.248.
subfiles.summary: Largely blank enclosure charge slip for file 894.248, with no legible borrower or date.

subfiles.title: FBI cover letter on Japanese aircraft output and German submarines
subfiles.about: Hoover forwards confidential foreign-source information on Japanese aircraft production and German submarine technology.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends Berle an enclosed memorandum obtained from an ordinarily reliable source abroad. He notes that the same information was furnished to William J. Donovan, the Board of Economic Warfare, naval intelligence, and military intelligence. Page 25 is a duplicate or carbon version of the cover letter.

subfiles.title: Confidential information on Japanese aircraft output and German submarine developments
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr. and designated intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports high estimates of Japanese aircraft production and claims about new German submarine propulsion and oxygen-generation systems.
subfiles.summary: An English aircraft expert estimates Japanese 1941 output at 34,000 engines and 12,000-16,000 planes, above other estimates, with enough aluminum and bauxite; a separate report claims Germany developed a single submarine motor and onboard hydrogen and oxygen production.

subfiles.title: Improvement in Japanese aircraft
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports changes to the Zero fighter and a better-armed Japanese bomber used at high altitude.
subfiles.summary: FBI source: the old Zero was replaced; production includes a better-armed bomber, the new Zero is maneuverable but lightly armored with wing failures in dives, and Japanese planes bombing Darwin and Port Moresby flew too high for P-39s and P-40s.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on arms exports to China and Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to figures on licenses for exporting arms and implements of war to China and Japan from 1937 through 1941.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a letter giving the value of arms export licenses to China and Japan, January 1937 to December 1941.

subfiles.title: Departmental memorandum on London despatch No. 6450
subfiles.about: The memorandum calls attention to a London despatch estimating Japanese production capacity at 1,000–1,200 aircraft per month.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs summarizes John Allison's memorandum on Japanese air strength; the reported 1,000-1,200 aircraft monthly exceeds usual estimates but was circulated.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 6450: Japan’s Air Strength
subfiles.from: Ware Adams, for the U.S. Ambassador in London
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards John Allison’s study and related British documents on Japanese aircraft production and air strength.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 6450 sends Allison's memorandum, Emil Speyer's letter and Colonel Vickers's comments; a British economic-warfare official privately put Japanese output at no less than 1,000 and probably 1,200 planes monthly, not the Ministry's or Air Ministry's final estimate.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan’s Air Strength
subfiles.about: Allison reviews conflicting British estimates of Japanese aircraft output and reports new evidence suggesting production of at least 1,000 planes per month.
subfiles.summary: Allison contrasts Speyer's 12,000-16,000 annual aircraft with British estimates of 4,000-5,000; Murray's machine-tool analysis suggests 1,000-1,200 monthly, sustaining 5,000 first-line planes; a possible crankshaft bottleneck; a Japanese Aviation Industry Association formed.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Aircraft Industry
subfiles.about: Speyer argues that prevailing Allied estimates greatly understated Japan’s aircraft and aero-engine production.
subfiles.summary: Speyer's published letter extrapolates prewar figures to 34,000 engines and 12,000-16,000 aircraft yearly in 1941, says aluminum and bauxite suffice, citing Korea, Palau and the East Indies, and says Japan is wrongly seen as a textile producer.

subfiles.title: Colonel Vickers’s comments on Speyer’s aircraft-production estimates
subfiles.about: The memorandum rejects Speyer’s extrapolation methods and presents substantially lower British estimates of Japanese aircraft production.
subfiles.summary: Vickers says Speyer lacked Japan experience; British estimates were about 1,800 aircraft in 1935-1936 and 4,000-5,000 now, some sources 8,800-11,400, with no evidence for 12,000-16,000; he agrees only on raw materials and underestimated industrial strength.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japan’s aircraft position as of June 30, 1943
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a despatch enclosing a March 1944 memorandum and translation on Japan’s aircraft position as of June 30, 1943.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference points to Chungking despatch No. 2334 concerning Japan’s aircraft position on June 30, 1943. The despatch reportedly enclosed a memorandum dated March 16, 1944 and a translated report. Page 41 records that the material was sent to PA/H without record.
